doc.title: Tom Lellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 31, 2007

chapter: Career, business and the music industry
title: Business people, American Idol and the decline of quality
summary: He blames business graduates and promotion over craft for the music scene, noting record heads used to be musicians, and dismisses Rod Stewart's standards.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Do you think the American Idol syndrome and stuff plays into that?

Well that’s like — well I’ll tell you a bigger overview is that I think that business has conspired to bring the masses into music. They want the masses to — you know they want you to be a singer. They want everyone to be able to sing. So now instead of to get to Carnegie Hall you practice, practice, practice, now you, like they promoted the pet rock, you just promote something until it’s so popular you can buy Carnegie Hall. And that’s how I feel about it. I feel that the quality that the great musicians that you’ve interviewed and that we all know have spent these years trying to hone a craft and all of a sudden that quality doesn’t matter. It’s not about that anymore. It’s about something else. And that something else is a scandalous scheme, a businessman’s dream — that’s a lyric that’s coming.

And that’s what it is. I feel that all these Harvard graduates, business graduates, they’re going well why do I want to deal with a temperamental artist. Let me create Milli Vanilli. And so I blame, you know, in a culture the tallest things in that culture are the most important things. And it used to be churches and now it’s Citi Corps.
Now it’s what? © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
City Corps, you know, or you know what I mean? Corporate buildings. So they have that bottom line. And that bottom line and art, they don’t mix, they shouldn’t mix.
Some fellows that I talked to, had pointed out that years ago the heads of the record companies were musicians.
And that they felt it made a big difference.

Well it does. That’s what I’m saying. These business, Harvard business graduates, they learn to sell anything. So why do they want to deal with temperamental quality? Or maybe not even temperamental, they don’t know. They were trained in business. They weren’t trained in music. So maybe they like, maybe they think the sun sets with Bruce Springsteen.
What’s your — I played a gig a couple of months ago and some woman said to me, “We want to hear those older songs, those Rod Stewart songs.”
Right. There’s another one. I didn’t mention him, should have.
I said Rod Stewart songs, then I finally figured out what she was talking about, you know.
Oh the standards album that he recorded.

Right. You know I say well let me say, let me drink booze for about twenty years and have a little sip of hydrochloric acid and then I’ll go into the studio. That’s what it would take for me to get to that place. And I just reject it totally.
